title: Forecast Evaluation
learning_outcomes: Explain forecast evaluation and accurately refer to at least two syllabus subtopics.
Apply the main idea of forecast evaluation to a small example, trace, calculation, or scenario.
Identify one important assumption or failure mode and describe how to check it.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will study forecast evaluation in the context of time-series analysis and forecasting. You will connect the PDF subtopics to a small example and practice describing what the evidence does—and does not—support.
content.why_it_matters: Forecast Evaluation matters because it affects how data is collected, represented, analyzed, interpreted, or used in a decision. Check the task and assumptions before choosing a method.

content_blocks.title: The central idea
content_blocks.text: Time-dependent data must be evaluated in temporal order. Trend, seasonality, calendar effects, and structural changes can make random splitting misleading.

items.title: Forecast horizon
items.text: Define forecast horizon in relation to forecast evaluation; identify the input, output, assumptions, and who uses the result.

items.title: Rolling-origin validation
items.text: Work through rolling-origin validation using a small, synthetic example before scaling up. State what the calculation or method returns and why that result is useful.

items.title: MAE and RMSE
items.text: Check the edge cases for mae and rmse: missing values, unusual ranges, different groups, time boundaries, or a changed input can affect the conclusion.

items.title: Percentage-based metrics and their limitations
items.text: Document the rule or choice for percentage-based metrics and their limitations so another learner can reproduce the analysis and understand its limitations.

items.title: Prediction intervals
items.text: Define prediction intervals in relation to forecast evaluation; identify the input, output, assumptions, and who uses the result.

content_blocks.title: Guided walkthrough
content_blocks.text: 1. Restate the question addressed by forecast evaluation. 2. Identify the input data, intended output, and assumptions. 3. Predict what the small example should show before reading its output. 4. Change one input or assumption, compare the result, and document what remains uncertain.

content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the provided synthetic input, rerun or retrace the example, and change one value at a time. Do not use personal records, credentials, or data you are not authorized to access.

content_blocks.title: Common mistakes and fixes
content_blocks.text: Keep the question, data grain, units, and assumptions explicit. If a result differs, inspect the input and steps in order. Avoid turning an observed association into a causal claim, treating a sample as the population, or assuming a small demonstration guarantees production behavior. A moving average smooths short-term variation but can lag sudden changes.

content_blocks.title: Responsible interpretation
content_blocks.text: This example is a teaching aid. It is static in the CodeLeaf lesson and is not executed in the browser. It uses small synthetic values; validate any real workflow in a separate, appropriate local environment and protect sensitive data.

content_blocks.title: Recap and next step
content_blocks.text: Recap: Time-dependent data must be evaluated in temporal order. Trend, seasonality, calendar effects, and structural changes can make random splitting misleading. Next, connect this lesson to the linked prerequisite or following lesson. Record the method, input assumptions, observed result, and one limitation so another person can reproduce and review the work.

content.task: Try it yourself: create a small synthetic example for forecast evaluation. State a question, make a prediction, trace or run an appropriate calculation, then write one finding and one limitation.
task_acceptance_criteria: Refer accurately to the topic and its syllabus subtopics.
Record a reproducible example or a complete manual trace with an expected result.
Document at least one assumption, limitation, data-quality issue, or evaluation check.
hints: Write down the input, expected result, units, and assumptions first.
Change only one condition when testing a revised example.
Ask whether the data and method represent the real decision; do not infer causality or production readiness from a toy example.
troubleshooting: Check input values, path assumptions, package versions, indentation, and units.
